extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and medical/psychology practitioners interested in perception and psychopathology
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conceptual markers for identifying, characterizing, and explaining sensory hallucinations (their forms, causes, progression, and consequences) in clinical, experimental, and historical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of hallucination
rubrics_metrics.description: “By hallucination is meant, in scientific phraseology, such a false perception of one or other of the senses as a person has when he sees, hears, or otherwise perceives as real what has no outward existence — that is to say, has no existence outside his own mind, is entirely subjective.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as the baseline diagnostic notion: a hallucination is a perception without an external stimulus. The article illustrates with historical (Joan of Arc) and clinical examples to show both genuine conviction and absence of external referent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence and conviction despite contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Patients may insist that hallucinated perceptions are as real as ordinary perceptions and remain unconvinced by argument or demonstration to the contrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the man who smells foul odors from his body and the man who hears abusive voices — both resist logical refutation. This perceptual certainty is a key sign distinguishing hallucination from mere error or misreport.

rubrics_metrics.name: All sensory modalities can be affected
rubrics_metrics.description: “Each sense may of course be affected, and sight stands next to hearing in its liability to suffer.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect olfactory, auditory, visual, tactile and gustatory hallucinations in various conditions (e.g., delirium tremens, melancholia, nervous disorders). Examples: visions of reptiles in delirium tremens, voices in auditory hallucination, tactile ‘blows’ or tastes of poison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuum / gradation from transient disturbances to full hallucination
rubrics_metrics.description: There are gradational states between the most extreme hallucinations and such temporary disorders of the senses as healthy persons often have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use transient, stimulus-linked sensations (e.g., giddiness and ringing after stooping) and early fever experiences as evidence of a continuum. Clinically, assess whether the phenomenon is transient/physiological or progressive/psychopathological.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological mechanisms (e.g., congestion/stimulation of nerve-centres)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some hallucinations are due to stimulation of respective nerve-centres by a congestion of blood in the brain (example: stooping with head hanging low produces ringing, flashes, even brief figures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider reversible physiological causes (positional, circulatory, febrile) before attributing hallucinations to fixed psychiatric disease. This is particularly relevant for transient or situational hallucinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progression pattern in febrile/delirious states
rubrics_metrics.description: At the beginning of a fever the patient may be aware that strange faces are not real; later the hallucinations come more often, the patient becomes uncertain, and eventually they gain entire mastery so that he cannot distinguish between them and real figures (wild delirium).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this staged progression to evaluate severity and prognosis: initial insight -> increasing frequency/ubiquity -> loss of reality-testing = progression toward delirium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production by vivid idea or imagination (suggestive/intense conception)
rubrics_metrics.description: A vividly-conceived idea which is so intense that it appears to be an actual perception, a mental image so vivid that it becomes a visual image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute some hallucinations to strong imagery/imagination (artists, writers, creative geniuses). Examples: mesmeric demonstrations, Newton/Blake/Dickens anecdotes; these may occur in sane individuals but can become pathological if persistent or uncontrollable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mesmeric / suggestive induction of perceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: In the so-called mesmeric state suggestion by an operator can make subjects taste, see, or feel things (e.g., tasting water as bitter or sweet, imagining bees and reacting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat reports emerging under suggestion or hypnosis with caution; expectancy and suggestion can produce genuine-seeming sensory experiences without external stimulus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association of multisensory impressions in perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception of a particular object is formed by association of the sensations it excites in our different senses; the visual impression is 'a sign' to which experience gives meaning (example: idea of an orange combines taste, touch, smell, sight).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the associative model to understand how memory and prior multisensory experience can supply missing sensory information and thereby produce misperception or hallucination when one modality is activated or imagined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominion of the idea over sense (preconception bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a man has a foregone conclusion of what he will see, it is not safe to trust his observation implicitly; the idea in the mind will affect the perception and cause mistaken perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For evaluating eyewitness or clinical reports, assess the subject's expectations and hypotheses. Scientific observers must guard against confirmation bias and preconception-induced errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solitary confinement and lack of mental resources as risk factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Auditory hallucinations are apt to occur in prisoners subjected to long periods of solitary confinement: brooding thoughts, not distracted by others, become audible as actual voices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider environmental and social deprivation as etiological factors when auditory hallucinations arise in otherwise intact individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural/historical congruence of hallucinated content
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparitions and hallucinations tend to reflect the dominant ideas or beliefs of the age (examples: witches on broomsticks in eras believing in witchcraft; Satan apparitions in the Middle Ages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting content, take into account cultural expectations and prevailing belief-systems; content congruence can inform but does not prove external reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential adverse outcomes of persistent hallucinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Persistent, uncontrollable hallucinations may lead to loss of sanity, melancholy, despair, and even suicide (illustrated by cases of a painter confined in an asylum and a man who shot himself because haunted by his double).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use severity and persistence as criteria for urgency of intervention; note that vivid imaginative faculties may be a risk factor if not controllable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stages of degradation of consciousness under chloroform
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary observations: (1) sensations from special senses cease earliest; then impression of external force and consciousness of external space-relations cease; (2) a vague sense of relative position within the body may remain, fading to sensations implied by the heart's pulsations; (3) the cluster produced by the heart's action may constitute the only remaining portion of the ego; (4–9) on returning consciousness, a sense of pressure appears (not proper cognition), pain is universal then later localizes vaguely, and appearances (e.g., 'the girl') may arise without conceptual recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these empirical markers when characterizing anesthesia-induced changes in consciousness: order of loss and return of sensory and cognitive components yields insight into the structure of consciousness and can be used to interpret subjective reports under anaesthesia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localization vs universality of sensations during transition states
rubrics_metrics.description: During anaesthesia or other altered states pain or sensation may be 'universal instead of local' at first, and when localization occurs its spatial position is vague (example: localized as 'up on the right').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing subjective reports from altered-consciousness states, expect early diffuse sensations that later become localized but remain imprecise; such features inform whether reported experiences are genuine localized nociception or global altered-state phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing perception from interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeing is one thing and the interpretation thereof quite another; people may have seen apparitions but have interpreted them according to prevailing beliefs — hence what is reported is perception plus interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating testimony, separate the raw sensory report from the interpretive layer (religious, cultural, personal meaning). This helps avoid conflating hallucination content with ontological claims about external agents.
